issues.legal_issue: An arbitral award is not open to correction for factual mistakes or an alleged error in applying the law unless an erroneous legal proposition appears in the award or an incorporated document and forms the basis of the award.
material_facts: The award stated the requirement under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act that a transferee must have performed or be willing to perform his part of the contract.
The award found that the party in possession had stopped paying the monthly instalments and was not willing to perform that obligation.
The challenge alleged that the arbitrator had erred by treating the monthly payments as still due after the other contracting party repudiated the agreement.
The award contained no erroneous statement of the legal requirement; the alleged error concerned its application to the circumstances.
issues.conclusion: The objection did not establish an error of law on the face of the award, so the award was not set aside on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 30 and 33 of the Arbitration Act, 1940, an error of law is reviewable when an erroneous legal proposition appears in the award or a document incorporated into it and forms the basis of the award; a mistake of fact is not reviewable merely because a court might assess the facts differently. The court relied on Coimbatore District Podu Thozillar Sangam v. Balasubramania Foundary, Champsey Bhara and Co. v. Jivraj Balloo Spinning and Weaving Co. Ltd., Kanpur Nagar Mahapalika v. M/s Narain Das Haribansh, State of Orissa v. M/s Lall Brothers, and Union of India v. A. L. Rallia Ram. Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act requires a transferee invoking its protection to have performed or be willing to perform his part of the contract.

rule.if: arbitration_award_challenge and award_states_correct_legal_requirement and challenged_error_concerns_application_or_facts and no_erroneous_legal_proposition_in_award

predicates.arbitration_award_challenge: A party seeks to set aside or correct an arbitrator’s award.
predicates.award_states_correct_legal_requirement: The award sets out the legal requirement relevant to the dispute without stating it incorrectly.
predicates.challenged_error_concerns_application_or: The alleged error concerns how the arbitrator applied the legal requirement to the facts or assessed the facts.
predicates.no_erroneous_legal_proposition_in_award: The award and any document incorporated into it contain no erroneous legal proposition that forms the basis of the decision.

issues.definition: When an award challenge concerns the application of a correctly stated legal requirement or the assessment of facts, and the award contains no erroneous legal proposition forming its basis, the award is not set aside for error on its face.

issues.legal_issue: A party faced with an anticipatory breach may either treat the contract as ended and seek damages or keep it alive and seek specific performance, but the latter course requires readiness and willingness to perform the party’s own obligations.
material_facts: One contracting party repudiated the agreement before the parties had completed their mutual obligations.
The party seeking to rely on the agreement argued that the repudiation excused further performance of its own obligations while it continued to rely on the contract.
That party had not continued making the required monthly payments, and the award found it was not willing to perform its obligation.
issues.conclusion: Anticipatory breach did not excuse the party from showing readiness and willingness to perform when it sought to keep the contract alive and claim specific performance.
issues.legal_principle: A party may treat an anticipatory breach as ending the contract and sue for damages, but cannot then seek specific performance. Alternatively, the party may keep the contract alive until the time for performance and seek specific performance, but must show readiness and willingness to perform. International Contractors Ltd. v. Prasanta Kumar Sur was distinguished: it did not dispense with the readiness-and-willingness requirement, although in certain circumstances it may not be necessary to tender the remaining performance in the contractual manner.

rule.if: contract_specific_performance_dispute and anticipatory_breach and claimant_keeps_contract_alive and claimant_seeks_specific_performance and not claimant_ready_and_willing

predicates.contract_specific_performance_dispute: The dispute concerns a claim for specific performance of a contract.
predicates.anticipatory_breach: One contracting party repudiates the contract before the time for performance or before mutual obligations are completed.
predicates.claimant_keeps_contract_alive: The party seeking relief elects to treat the contract as continuing rather than ending it for breach.
predicates.claimant_seeks_specific_performance: The claimant asks the court to enforce the contract by specific performance.
predicates.claimant_ready_and_willing: The claimant is ready and willing to perform the claimant’s own contractual obligations.

issues.definition: If a claimant keeps a contract alive after an anticipatory breach and seeks specific performance without being ready and willing to perform, specific performance is unavailable.

issues.legal_issue: An award is not set aside for failing to discuss documents unless the challenge establishes that material documents necessary to resolve the dispute were not considered or otherwise establishes legal misconduct.
material_facts: The challenging party asserted that important documents had not been referred to or discussed in the award.
The party did not identify a particular document shown to be essential to resolving the dispute or demonstrate that such a document had not been considered.
The challenge was framed as an error of law on the face of the award, not as legal misconduct by the arbitrator.
issues.conclusion: The contention that documents had been omitted was unsupported and did not provide a basis for setting aside the award.
issues.legal_principle: K. P. Poulose v. State of Kerala and Another recognizes that failure to consider material documents necessary for a just and fair resolution may amount to legal misconduct. That principle did not assist the challengers because they did not identify or establish the omission of any essential document, and their objection was not based on misconduct.

rule.if: arbitration_award_challenge and appellant_alleges_documents_were_omitted and not essential_omitted_document_demonstrated and not legal_misconduct_established

predicates.arbitration_award_challenge: A party seeks to set aside or correct an arbitrator’s award.
predicates.appellant_alleges_documents_were_omitted: The challenging party alleges that the arbitrator failed to consider or discuss documents.
predicates.essential_omitted_document_demonstrated: The challenging party identifies and demonstrates that an omitted document was essential to resolving the dispute.
predicates.legal_misconduct_established: The challenging party establishes that the arbitrator’s conduct amounted to legal misconduct.

issues.definition: When a party alleges that documents were omitted but demonstrates neither an essential omitted document nor legal misconduct, the award is not set aside for document omission.
